George
Be n s o n
From the very beginning,
the sound of the guitar
was always in my mind.
From the moment I heard
it, I knew that my life was
going to have something
to do with the guitar. I did
not know I was going to be
a player yet, but I loved the
sound.
                                    68
                           46




 As I grew older, I began to dabble with the guitar, to pick it up and try to pick things out. I would get so far, and
 then I would get stuck. I have found later that this is normal. Everybody goes through that on every instrument.
 To move forward, you have to take in more information, and look at things from different angles or from a dif-
 ferent point of view. So I started asking questions from the people whom I knew that had a certain mastery of the
 instrument.

 In my home town of Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, a lot of traveling groups would come through town and I always went up
 to the guitar player to ask if he could show me something. I was never too ashamed to ask. The George Benson you
 know today is a collection of all those people who took the time to show me what they knew, and the things I could
 hang on to did me a lot of good.

 From guitar books, which I was not a reader, I was more of a picture guy. But the demonstrations in the new books
 really helped a lot to show the correct fingerings for this, that, and the other. They showed how to make chords.
 The chords led me to the harmony, that helped me to become a better single line player.

       Peter Farrell
                                  68
                           46




          Peter Farrell was born in Sao Paulo, Brazil in 1981. Son of the singer Claudia Fier and the
          saxophone player Lino Simão. He began studying music at school very young with an early
          interest in flute & violin.

          Still very young, his mother introduced him to the jazz and classical worlds, giving him the
          opportunity to hear the music of George Benson, Antonio Carlos Jobim, Debussy, Ravel,
          Bach, Dori Caymmi, Toninho Horta, Bill Evans, Herbie Hancock and many others.

          However, just like every teenager, Peter loved rock’n’roll and at the age of 11 he asked his
          mother to take him to a guitar teacher. So he began studying guitar with José Walter, which
          gave him the first basic steps to rock and blues.

                              2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
the George Benson Method                                                                                    4668




            One year later, the young boy was taken by his aunt Léa Freire and his uncle Sizão Mach-
            ado to a music conservatory called Groove, where he studied classical guitar, music
            theory, and jazz guitar with Leyve Miranda and Luis Cavalcante. In this period Peter
            started going deep into the music of George Benson and Wes Montgomery.

            Also in this period, Peter studied Brazilian music with the extraordinary guitar player Lula
            Galvão, and also piano with the great pianist and arranger Edmundo Cassis, who gave him
            a new vision about harmony.

            After many years of studying day and night, Peter started giving his first lessons and re-
            alized he had a great talent to teach and encourage others. Since then teaching has also
            become his passion.

            It did not take long until musicians all over the world started keeping their eyes on him
            because of his ability, technique and musicality. He was very advanced for an 18 year old
            boy. As a matter of fact, Peter was known in the musical scene as a prodigy since he was 14.

            Sometime later Peter was introduced to his idol and mentor George Benson. The connec-
            tion between them was instantaneous. The great Benson was amazed at Peter’s talent and
            how he had decoded many of his secrets. After a few months of friendship, Peter became
                                    68


            Mr. Benson’s private student and it has continued for the past 15 years.

            During the last six years Peter Farrell and George Benson have been dedicated to this col-
                           46




            lection of method books that they have created together: The George Benson Method.

            Peter Farrell has recorded and played with many great artists all over the world such as Jane
            Monheit, Brian McKnight, Eumir Deodato, Cesar Camargo Mariano, Romero Lubambo,
            Adam Rogers, and Didier Lockwood just to name a few.

How to use this book
Although a big part of this method is exclusively dedicated to the guitar, (because it refers to
chord construction and basic visualization of the guitar fretboard),it was created as a tool for all
instruments of all levels (beginner, intermediate and advanced). However, even if you are an
advanced player, make sure you know start at the beginning of the book, otherwise you will
easily get lost by the end of the book.


This method should be used as a dictionary of ideas and techniques. It's important to understand
that the way we approach the musical concepts, ideas and techniques presented here are unique
and cannot be found elsewhere.


Do not worry about learning everything from every chapter. You can go ahead as soon as you
understand the concepts. But always remember that you can come back to any chapter of any
book in order to learn more about a determined subject you want to study again.


Be careful when trying to learn too much at one time. Music is not about quantity but quality.



George and I have been working for many years on this giant collection of books to give you the
                               68


best we can and help those that love the guitar the way we do. We hope this method can open a
new world that was unknown until now. You have a treasure in your hands. It contains all the
knowledge that George Benson has been teaching me privately over the last 15 years.
                      46




Thanks a lot,


Peter Farrell

                                              Important device:
The patterns and scale visualizations in this book may have different time signatures in order to
help with the organization and visualization. Notice that depending on where and how we play
them on the fretboard, we will have more or less possibilities. Don’t let the time signatures
confuse you. Learn the ideas that you like the most and apply them where you feel they sound
the best. Give more attention to the single lines shown.

    Harmony Knowledge and Rules

    Harmonic Regions for Major Keys
    The Harmonic Regions de1ine and organize the roles of each chord with regard to the key
    of a song, in addition to providing various replacement options for each of them. We have
    3 harmonic regions: ("C" major as reference)


    1- Root Region Chords (Tonic): Cmaj7 (I), Em7 (IIIm), Am7 (VIm).
    2- Subdominant Region Chords: (this group in divided into two groups):
    • Major: Fmaj7 (IV), Dm7 (IIm), Bbmaj7 (bVII).
    • Minor: Fm7(6) (7+) (IVm), Bb7 (bVII), Abmaj7 (bVI), Dbmaj7 (bII).

    3- Dominant Region Chords: G7 (V), Bø (VII).
                                  68


    Functions of the Harmonic Regions:
                         46




    • Root Region(Tonic):
     It gives the sense of resolution, rest or "being home" (key).

    • Subdominant Region:
     It gives the sense of movement and distancing, moving away from the tonic.

    • Dominant Region:
    It gives the sense of tension and instability, and wants to resolve to the tonic. With these three
    functions ( IV / V / I = distancing, tension and rest ), we generate what we call a cadence, which
    is a chord progression with a resolution effect that defines the music's path. So let's understand
    some aspects of this:

Possibilities of Chord voicings:
                                                                                           4668




• Major 7th chords:
 Cmaj7, Cmaj7(9), C6 , C6(9), Cmaj7(#11), C6(#11) , C6(9)#11, Cmaj7(6), Cmaj7(6)9



• Minor 7th chords:
 Cm7, Cm7(9), Cm7(11), Cm7(9)11, Cm(maj7)9, Cm6, Cm6(9)



• Half Diminished chords:
 Dø, Dø(9), Dø(11), Dø(9)11, Dm7(b6)



• Dominant 7th chords leading to major chords (V degree):
 G7, G7(9), G7(b9), G7(#9), G7(13), G7(b13), G7(b9)b13, G7(#9)b13, G7(9)13,
 G7(b9)13, G7(#11), G7(b9)#11, Gsus9, Gsus13, Gsus(b9)
                            68



• Dominant 7th chords leading to minor chords (V degree):
                   46




 G7, G7(b9), G7(#9), G7(b9)13, G7(b13), G7(b9)b13, G7(#11), G7(b9)#11, Gsus(b9),
 Gsus9


Attention:
Dominant 7th chords that are not the Vth degree or a tritone substitution, are always
considered lydian dominant. In other words, we can use the following tensions on them:

• 9, 13, or #11. Even though this is a rule, remember that it can be broken, mainly when
we have modal harmonies. (we will explore modal and tonal harmonies later).



                        2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved              2
    Substitution Chords using Harmonic Regions:                                                           4668




    In theory, any chord of a given Harmonic Region may be replaced by another of the same region.
    Hence we will find the most famous cadence in popular music: IIm / V/ I. But notice that we
    had to replace the IVth degree by the IIm, which belongs to the same region.
    It is important to understand that a cadence does not have to be completed all the time.
    Sometimes we cannot play II / V/ I in the same bar, therefore we can simply play V/ I. Actually,
    a subdominant chord is used to delay the Dominant chord, giving more colors to the harmony.
    In addition to the substitutions we can make between chords derived from the same Harmonic
    Region,we can also go deeper with substitutions by replacing chords derived from the Dominant
    Region with the ones derived from the Major or Minor Subdominant Region.

    Attention in the exercises below:
    a) I covers all the chords derived from the Root Region.
    b) V covers all the chords derived from the Dominant Region.
    c) IV covers all the chords derived from the Subdominant Region.

Harmonic Regions for Minor Keys
                                                                                                      4668




In minor keys we may use the Harmonic Regions as follows (“Cm” as reference):

1- Root Region Chords: Cm7 (I), Ebmaj7 (bIII)



2- Subdominant Region Chords: Fm7(6) (7+) (IVm), Bb7 (bVII), Abmaj7 (bVI),
                              Dbmaj7 (bII), Dø (II)


3- Dominant Region Chords: G7 (V), B˚ (VII)


Attention:

In minor keys the chords of the Dominant Region can be replaced by the chords of the Minor
Subdominant Region. Moreover, in a more modern view, we can also use the chords belonging
to the Minor Subdominant Region of the relative major key to replace the chords from the
Dominant Region. The examples given here are in the key of Cm, so we would use the chords
of the Minor Subdominant Region of "Eb" major replacing the chords from the Dominant
Region (G7, B˚).
                               68


4- Minor Subdominant Region from the Major Relative (Eb):
                     46




  Abm7(6) (7+) (IVm), Db7 (bVII), Bmaj7 (bVI), Emaj7 (bII).


An important detail to notice in the cadence II/V/I in minor keys (IVm/V7/Im) is that the
dominant seventh chords almost always use altered tensions such as: b9, # 9, # 11, b13. The
major 13th can be used with some regularity in the chords, but it is still an exception. In the key
of Cm we can have the cadence: G7(b9)13 leading to Cm7 for example.

Even though there are many possibilities, we can never forget that the most important thing
when comping is to follow the melody, which will “tell” us what the best chord options are.
However, when improvising we can be more free because we will create the melodies, so it
means that even if we have a pre-set harmony dictated by the music, we can use all the “colors”
we have learned before, playing single notes or even block chords.

Major & Minor - II / V / I – Progression                                                             4668




• Basic Major II / V / I Progression:                         Dmi7          G7        Cmaj7    ‘
• Basic Minor II / V / I Progression:                         Dª            G7        Cmi7     ‘

It is important to understand that any tension note applyed over these chords (7, 9, 11, 13), does
not affect their function in any way. Actually the tension notes are used to "color" the cadence.

Similarity between the major and the minor II/V/I cadences:
Despite being apparently two very different chord progressions, there is a huge correlation
between the major and the minor II/V/I cadences. Therefore, in order to better understand that
idea, let's analize them degree by degree for comparison.

The comparison between both cadences can only work if we use them in the right keys. Let’s
use the keys of “C” major and “Am”, because they are relatives and this is the beginning of the
similarity we are looking for. See below:

•     Dmi7       G7      Cmaj7          ‘                 •          Bª        Emi7     Ami7   ‘

II degree = Dm7 is a dorian chord, which means that it could be Dm6 as well. Now comes the
tricky thing: the third inversion of Dm6 is Bø which is the II degree from the Am cadence. So
we conclude that both II degree are the same.
                                68


V degree = Considering that G7(b9) is an option of the V chord leading to C major, and E7(b9)
is an option of the V degree leading to Am, we can compare them properly. So, first of all we
                      46




must understand that G7(b9) is the same chord as Ab˚ with a different root. See below:

• G7(b9) : G, B, D, F, Ab           • Ab˚ : Ab, B, D, F

The diminished chord repeats itself every minor 3rd. So Ab˚ = B˚= D˚ = F˚. Now let's
understand that E7(b9)/B is the same chord as B˚. So, finally we have Ab˚ = B˚ or G7(b9) =
E7(b9). Other tensions applied over these 2 dominant 7th chords can work with this comparison
as well, but the flat 9 is the best example. Later on we will better understand that correlation
between both cadences.

I degree = “Am” is the relative minor of “C major”, therefore the same chord (C6).

Conclusion: We may then conclude that both II/V/I progressions can be considered the
same depending on the treatment given to the chords.

    Secondary Dominant                                                                                                                                         4668




    As we know, dominant 7th chords resolve to their ‘I’ chord. However, in the diatonic chord
    series, we have only one dominant chord, (G7) and it resolves to the tonic chord (C). So,
    secondary dominants are dominant chords that resolve to the other harmonic >ield degrees.
    They don't belong to the harmonic >ield and have nothing to do with it, except for the chord
    that they were assigned to resolve to. See the example below:

Notice that, for a matter of organization and didatic, we apply dominant chords with altered
notes only for minor degrees. But actually, we can use any alteration to any dominant chord
leading to major or minor. However, we must make sure the altered notes we choose can be
applied over the song we are playing, because the melody will always determine what we
can and can not use. On the other hand, when we are improvising, we are much more free to
add any chord substitution in order to create movement and tension to the solo.

Notice that dominant 7th chords such as 7(b9), 7(#9), and 7(b13), can be considered as
being the same, therefore they have the same function. Another important thing to notice
is that depending on the dominant chord we apply the tritone substitution to, it may not
sound correct or great. Example:

• C7(9) using a tritone substitution would be Gb7(b13), which most of time does not work.
So we replace the Gb7(b13) by Gb7(#11). However, in a cadence leading to Fmaj7 such
|| Gm7 | C7(9) | Fmaj7 || we should also change the voicing from the 1st chord as well.
Therefore, we would have: || Gm7(11) | Gb7(#11) | Fmaj7 ||.

     Diminished Chords have an interesting characteristic, they repeat themselves every minor
     3rd. In other words, for every diminished chord, we will always have four options.
     Example: "C˚" can be replaced by "Eb˚", "Gb˚" or "A˚", because they contain the same notes,
     therefore are the same chord. We have 2 different cases:

     1) Fake Diminished Chord:
     This type of diminished chord can be analyzed as an inverted dominant 7th (b9) chord.
     Below we have as example an A7(b9) chord which has the intervals: Root, b7, b9, 3, from
     low to high in the order they appear, followed by 4 diminished chords that are inversions
     of it. But to better understand this relashionship, let’s consider each interval from each
     diminished chord as belonging from A7. (Notice that the root note (A) was removed from
     the inverted chords, because there is no need for it). See below:


              A7≈                                             o                                  o                             o                              o
                                    =                 C#                                     E                             G                               B b
     Intervals related:                        (3, b7, b9, 5)                         (5, b9, 3, b7)                  (b7, 3, 5, b9)              (b9, 5, b7, 3)
     with A7(b9)

                      1   2fr.                            1           3fr.                       1       6fr.              1       2       5fr.                1       2       8fr.

In the old days, jazz musicians used to substitute the V, I progression (G7, C6) by VII7,
I (B7, C6). The reason why we can do this is quite simple: all the notes of B7 can work as
leading tones to the notes of C6, because they are half step from each other, creating a
sensation of tension and resolution. See below a visual explanation:


        B7               C6
                                             “Leading tone” table
                                             • "B" wants to resolve to "C"
                          ww
& # # www                ww
                                             • "F#" wants to resolve to "G"
        w                                    • "A" remains the same
                                             • "D#" wants to resolve to "E"

Note: With all this background, we can @inally understand why B7 can replace G7

Types of Musical Cadences:                                                                                  4668




Just like the rules of grammar, where we have paragraphs, periods, commas, punctuation,
exclamation and question marks, in music we have the same, but using sounds. For
example, a chord progression that ends in a dominant chord without resolution for
example, will surely give us the feeling of a question. Based on that, let's learn the 5 types
of cadences we can have:

Note: It is important to understand that the tension notes (7, 9, 11, 13) used over the chords
below do not affect their function in any way , they are just examples, which means that
we can have many other possibilities. Another important thing it is that when necessary,
the cadence II / V / I can be replaced by a simple V / I in major or minor keys.

1) Perfect Authentic Cadence:
A perfect authentic cadence is made from a subdominant chord plus a dominant chord
followed by the tonic chord (IV/V/I). Examples:

a)     G 713     Cmaj7                                       e)     G 7( b13)    Cmi 79
b)    Dmi 79      G 713      Cmaj 79       ‘                 f)       Dª         G7Ã          Cmi 79    ‘

     A plagal cadence is made from a subdominant chord followed by a tonic chord (IV /I). This

Tonal & Modal
  Harmony
      68
  46




  2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   24
     Summarizing, the term Tonal Harmony concerns harmonies formed by cadences and chord
                                                                                                   4668




     sequences that surround a particular key. On the other hand, the term Modal Harmony
     concerns harmonies that cannot have cadences, although there is a de@ined tonality as well.
     We can say that tonal and modal music have always been together, because even with the
     appearance of the tonal system in the Middle Ages, Modal Music was kept alive mainly in
     popular music and folk songs.

     However, modal music is much older than we think. It comes from ancient Greece, where
     each mode represented a state of mind, known as Ethos from the modes. It is important to
     understand that the pillar from the modal music is the melodic composition, where the
     composer creates melodies based on a determined mode. Therefore, what we call modal
     harmony came after modal music.

     After the Middle Ages, the interest for modal music was resumed in the Romantic Era with
     composers such Johannes Brahms and many others. Lately it has gotten strong with an
     artistic movement in Europe called "Impressionism". In music, it was led by two great
     composers named Claude Debussy and Maurice Ravel. Although we consider them as the
     main pillar from the Impressionism Era, actually this label was ignored by Debussy, and
     also was not well received by Ravel. They used to say that the term “impressionism” could
     not be used in music.

     Anyway, independent from names, that period brought to the music new horizons in terms
     of harmony, scales and atmospheres, but more than that in terms of art. The Impressionism
     movement intended to create new images and new sensations through exotic scales,
     chromatics, unconventional chord sequences, and unconventional chords, which were
     "treated" separately, and not as part of a sequence or harmonic chain. In other words, each
                                  68


     chord could receive a modal treatment independent of function or tonality. We call that
     feature “Modal Interchange”.
                         46




     However, we can have many discussions concerning modal and tonal harmonies, because
     we have some jazz songs that we can call "hybrid". When we say a song is hybrid, it is
     because it mixes modal harmony with tonal harmony at the same time. In other words, in
     one part it is modal and in the other part, it is tonal. The rule is quite simple: using
     cadences = Tonal Harmony, no cadences = Modal Harmony. However, some songs that we
     might consider modal are actually "hybrid" even without having cadences, because
     somehow the sequence of chords surround a determined key. Therefore, we can conclude
     that we have:

     1) Tonal Harmony
     2) Modal-Tonal Harmony
     3) Modal Harmony

     Modal Interchange
             &
      Parallel Modes
             68
        46




27       2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
                                                                                                   4668




After learning many types of cadences and chord substitutions, let’s add one more concept
to our harmonic knowledge: we'll call this “Modal Interchange”. It allows us to use some
chord substitutions giving each one of them a modal treatment. It is very similar to what
we have just learned about substitutions using the Harmonic Regions, but by using Modal
Interchange we can Eind new chords and also “colors” for the chords.

But in order to learn how to choose and apply the new chord possibilities, we must learn
about a new subject that we call “Parallel Modes”. Although it is related with a major
tonality and a minor tonality sharing the same tonic (“C”major and “C” minor, for example),
we can extend the concept by considering every mode sharing the the same tonic as a
parallel mode. See the example below:


• C (Ionian) → C (Aeolian) → C (Lydian) = Parallel Modes

Therefore, what we call modal interchange refers to borrowing chords from parallel modes
without abandoning the established key of the song. This concept has been used since the
Baroque era, and it is a tremendous asset for re-harmonizing songs, creating new “colors” to the
harmony, making them non predictable and much more interesting than just using the basic
chord sequences or progressions.




Modal Interchange Applied
                              68



In order to learn how to use modal interchange properly, we will use a table on the next
                     46




page that shows all the main modes and their diatonic chords. In the 1st column we have
the parallel modes and in the other columns we have the chords belonging to each mode.

It is important to understand that we will use what we have learned previously about
harmonic regions. So, in the table we have seven columns with the seven degrees that will
be divided into the three harmonic regions:


• Root region chords = I, III, VI

• Dominant region chords = V, VII

• Subdominant region chords = II, IV


                          2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved                    28
     In other words, it means that IN THEORY:                                                       4668




     1) in every I degree we can use chords belonging from the 1st , 3rd or 6th columns.

     2) in every II degree we can use chords belonging from the 2nd, 4th, 5th or 7th columns.

     3) in every III degree we can use chords belonging from the 3rd, 1st or 6th columns.

     4) in every IV degree we can use chords belonging from the 2nd, 4th, 5th or 7th columns.

     5) in every V degree we can use chords belonging from the 5th, 7th, 2nd or 4th columns.

     6) in every VI degree we can use chords belonging from the 6th, 1st or 3rd columns.

     7) in every VII degree we can use chords belonging from the 7th , 5th, 2nd or 4th columns.

Parallel Modes
  Exercises
      68
 46




  2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   32
     For the examples below, we will consider the concept of parallel modes, the way they are
                                                                                                   4668




     most known: a major key and a minor key sharing the same tonality. Example: "C" and Cm.
     We use this concept for improvising and also for re-harmonizing almost all the time,
     because most of western music uses this concept naturally.

     Well, let’s start using sequences of 2 chords. For now do not worry about tension notes or
     inversions, let’s focus on simple tetrads. It is important to understand that this exercise
     can only work using the major key as the guiding chord. In other words, the Girst chord of
     the sequence will always be from the major key, and all the other chords will be the
     degrees belonging to the parallel minor key. See below:


     Two chord Sequence Exercises: (“C” major key)

     1) | Cmaj7 |       Cm7      ||    → (major key) & I (1st degree from Cm key)

     2) | Cmaj7 |       Dø       ||     → (major key) & II (2nd degree from Cm key)

     3) | Cmaj7 | Ebmaj7 ||             → (major key) & bIII (3rd degree from Cm key)

     4) | Cmaj7 |       Fm7      ||     → (major key) & IV (4th degree from Cm key)

     5) | Cmaj7 |       Gm7       ||    → (major key) & V (5th degree from Cm key)
                                  68


     6) | Cmaj7 |     Abmaj7 ||          → (major key) & bVI (6th degree from Cm key)
                        46




     7) | Cmaj7 |      Bb7(9)     ||    → (major key) & bVII (7th degree from Cm key)



     Three or Four Chord Sequence Exercises: (“C” major key)

     Example 1:
     • || Cmaj7 |     Am7      | Fmaj7 |          %      || →      I , VI, IV

     Applying the parallel mode we would have:

     • || Cmaj7 | Abmaj7 |            Fm7    |    %     || → I , bVI, IVm


33                            2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
Example 2:                                                                                                 4668




From now on, we will start using extended notes on the chords, as the sequences will
become much more complex and the tensions become very important to create the right
voicings that link one chord to another. Below we have the second example:

• ||      Em7      |     Am7         |           Dm7        |        Gsus9     || →       III, VI, II, V

In the example below, in order to not lose the G7 as the V degree, we will consider it as
being G7(b13). Therefore, applying the parallel mode concept we would have:

• || Ebmaj7        |     Abmaj7      |            Dø        | G7(b13) ||
      bIII                bVI                      II            V7

Now, let’s use the Harmonic Region rules, that says that the dominant region chords and
the subdominant region chords are interchangeable. Below are the nomenclatures and
examples:
PM = Parallel Mode
Major SR = Major Subdominant Region
Minor SR = Minor Subdominant Region

• || Ebmaj7(9) |         Abmaj7          |       Dm7(9)         |     Fm6 ||
      bIII PM            bVI PM                  Major SR            Minor SR
We can also transform some degrees into dominant 7th chords, creating what we call:
" a blues vibe".
                                68


• || Ebmaj7(9) |          Ab7(13) |              Dbmaj7     |   Gsus9 ||
      bIII PM             bVI PM                 Minor SR   V7 original chord
                        46




                        (blues vibe)
• ||     Eb7(9)     |    Abmaj7          |       Fm7(9)       |   Gsus9 ||
          bIII PM        bVI PM                  Major SR     V7 original chord
       (blues vibe)
Now, let’s add one more element to the sequence: chord inversions:

• || Ebmaj7/Bb |          Abmaj7/C           |     Fmaj7/C          |   Fm6/C ||
      bIII PM              bVI PM                  Major SR             Minor SR

• || Ebmaj7/Bb | Am7(11)          |  Abmaj7                         |   Gsus9        ||
      bIII PM   VI original chord   Minor SR                        V7 original chord

Adding a New Chord Substitution Possibility                                                     4668




Just like we have learned and applied, the chords from the dominant region can be replaced by
the ones from the subdominant region (major or minor) and vice-versa. As we know, the minor
subdominant region is based on a minor chord which can be considered melodic minor if we
want. However, we should know that the chords derived from the melodic minor scale can
replace the dominant region chords with the subdominant region chords (major or minor), it
means that we can use the melodic minor chord family to replace the dominant region chords.
However, the melodic minor V degree chord might not work sometimes. For example if we
have a cadence Dm7,G7, Cmaj7 we could not use the C7(9/b13){V degree of F melodic minor}
to replace G7, because it has the same root note as the key (Cmaj7), and the cadence would
disappear: Dm7, C7(9/b13), Cmaj7.

     The minor II / V / I cadence is unique. It has two chords that can belong to the melodic minor
     family. Here is a Cm cadence as an example: Dø / G7 / Cm7. If we consider Dø chord as being
     locrian major 2nd we will have the VIth degree of F melodic minor, and if we consider the G7
     chord as being altered, we will have a VIIth degree of Ab melodic minor. Therefore, we
     already have many substitutions to apply even without changing the cadence order:
     subdominant, dominant, root. However we can do the same substitutions we did for the major
     II/V7/I, replacing the dominant chord with the subdominant melodic minor chord family.

     Turnaround Progression
     The turnaround progression is a II / V / I with an added chord: the VIth degree, which can be
     minor or dominant 7th depending on the harmonic situation. We have two different turnaround
     forms: - II / V / I / VI or I / VI / II / V. Basically we have major and minor turnaround
     progressions, however, the minor progression has 2 different options for the VIth degree, which
     are the VI7 or the bVI7. Below we have several examples of this new progression using many
     types of substitutions:

     "C" Major Turnaround Possibilities (I / VI / II / V)

     Chapter 4

     The Blues
     The Blues is a musical style and musical form considered "the father of jazz ". It was
     originated around the end of the 19th century by African Americans in the southern part of
     the United States. The genre is a merging of the african musical traditions, work songs,
     spirituals, Dield hollers, chants, and rhymed narrative ballads. The Blues has inDlueced many
     styles such as Jazz, R&B and Rock N' Roll, and it has some very speciDic characteristics. See
     below:


     1) It usually has 12 bar form;

     2) It has 2 different forms: Major Blues and Minor Blues;

     3) Harmonically, in its simple form, it is based on dominant 7th chords;

     4) It has its own scale that can summarize all the chords: The Blues Scale.
                                   68


     We can play the blues in a simple way, just like B.B King, Eric Clapton and SRV, or in a
     complex way, just like jazz musicians such Charlie Parker and John Coltrane did, using
     harmonic and melodic concepts coming from Classical Music.
                          46




     The blues teaches us how to “tell a story" through melodies and with improvisation, similar
     to question and answer by having an extremely organized structure, being easy and
     didactic to understand. It is the perfect place to start for those who wish to learn any style,
     melodically, harmonically and rhythmically speaking.

     The blues can have many harmonic variations, but let’s learn the most common ones. On
     the next pages we have two different Blues Forms (2 Major and 2 Minor), presented with
     roman numerals, which deDine the degrees to memorize and to distinguish them from each
     other. Snap your Dingers on beats 2 and 4, similar to what the drummer plays on the hi hat,
     then sing the degrees of each one of the shown blues forms. This is a very important step
     because we must know these forms inside and out without having to think about them.

Chapter 5                                                                                       4668




Open String Chords
We could say that the open string chords are the beginning and the ending path to learning
guitar chords. When we start playing, the 7irst thing we learn are the basic open string
chords such as "C" major, "E" major, "A"minor and so on. However, as soon as we have more
knowledge, we understand that they can be much more than just simple chords. Actually,
this type of chord family will create clusters that we cannot play without using at least one
open string.

How to Find the Open String Chord Possibilities:
Despite seeming to be very dif7icult to memorize and learn, the process to 7ind the open
string chord possibilities all over the guitar neck is quite simple to understand and apply.
There are 2 types of open string chords.

A) Chords that can only be played in a determined key and there is no possibility to create
   the same chord voicing in other keys.
B) Chords that can be played in many other keys, using the same chord voicing but losing
   all the open strings.

However, we can do some experimentation with all these chords by applying them on
                             68


different frets of the guitar fretboard, leaving at least one open string. The most common
open strings are the 1st and 2nd strings, but we can have examples using the 3rd or even
the 4th opened string.
                    46




Step 1:
Choose a chord shape leaving at least one open string.

Step 2:
After choosing the shape, apply it on every fret, thus analysing and checking what the best
sounding possibilities are. As a matter of fact, as time goes by we do not have to apply this
process everytime, because we will memorize which options are best and apply them in
the songs we know. It is important to understand that some open string chords might
repeat some of the notes within it. But sometimes the doubled notes can give an amazing
effect, mainly when we are playing arpeggios.

Pedal Point
      68
 46




  2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   168
  What is a Pedal Point ?                                                                             4668




  Pedal point, also known as pedal tone or pedal note, is a sustained note while other notes
  are moving. Usually, we use this concept to create a sequence of chords using the same
  bass note.

  However, we can use a pedal point to create sequences of chords that have the same note
  on the top. We call this an "inverted pedal". In addition to using this concept on the lower
  and higher notes, we can still use it for notes between the bass and the upper notes.

  This concept has been used since the early baroque era, and works to create tension in the
  harmony, breaking the monotony of common chords. On the guitar, we often use bass
  pedal points using open strings. We can apply it using the D, A or E strings. However, we
  can use what we call drop "D" tunning, which is tunning the E string into "D".

  Examples of Benson's songs using drop "D":
  a) Tenderly (from the album Tenderly)
  b) Ode to Kudu (from the album Weekend in L.A)



  The following chords are organized in 3 groups:
  a) Chords using the 6th string ("E" ) as pedal point
                                68


  b) Chords using the 5th string ("A" ) as pedal point
  c) Chords using Drop "D" as a pedal point
                       46




  Note: Most of the Drop "D" chords can be played also using the 4th string "D".

  The following chord examples are just a few of the many possibilities we can have. There are
  many other possibilities. It is important to understand that the pedal point chords can have many
  open strings or even the bass as the open string. Actually, they are part of the group of Open
  String Chords that change the type of the chord depending on the fret it is played on.

  The best way to use the pedal point chords or any open string chord, is to apply them as much
  as you can in every situation that is possible. It is advisable to apply them using simple and
  short sequences such as:

  1) I, IVm           2) I, VI, IIm, V               3) IV, IVm, I                  4) I, V

  Quartal Harmony
  Unlike tertian harmony, where the chords are built based on the superimposition of thirds,
  the concept of quartal harmony or quartal chord voicing is the stacking of superimposed
  4ths (perfect 4th, augmented 4th or diminished 4th). When we use this type of harmonic
  structure, the chords end up becoming hybrids, because they no longer sound major
  (happy), minor (sad) or even dominant (unstable), they just sound quartal, i.e. without a
  deAined characteristic.

  Example:
  If we have the chord:


  Dmi 74 (D (root) / G (perfect 4th / C (minor 7th) / F (minor 3rd)
             5fr.
         2
                               68


  It could be “D” Locryan, “D” Aeolian, “D” Dorian, or “D” Phrygian depending on the melody
  or bass note played over it.
                      46




  Although this had already been explored by composers of musical impressionism such as
  Debussy, Ravel and many others, in jazz the use of the quartal harmony became famous in
  the hands of the brilliant pianist McCoy Tyner, who developed the quartal voicings in a
  unique and wonderful way. We would suggest you listen to some speciAic albums where he
  gives us a lesson on how to use this kind of chord structure.
  a) A Love Supreme ( classic John Coltrane's recording )
  b) Reaching Fourths (McCoy Tuner's album Reaching Fourths)
  c) Impressions (McCoy Tuner's album Trident)
  But previous to the recordings of Tyner and Coltrane trumpet player and composer Miles
  Davis was a pioneer in the use of such harmony in jazz, when he launched, in August 1959,
  the album "Kind of Blue", one of the most brilliant albums in jazz history. In the well
  known composition "So What" by Miles Davis, we can hear very clearly the quartal
  voicings played by pianist Bill Evans.

201                        2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
The pentatonic scale has a very strong relationship with the Quartal Harmony, because its                                 4668




superimposed notes form quartal chord voicings. Within the major scale we can get three
possible major pentatonics: C major, G major, and F major. But let's exclude F major
pentatonic because it has the avoid note "F". Also remember that we can have the relative
minor pentatonic of each major pentatonic. So we have:

1) C major pentatonic: C, D, E, G, A                or    A minor pentatonic: A, C, D, E, G

2) G major pentatonic: G, A, B, D, E                or     E minor pentatonic: E, G, A ,B, D

Below we have some Quartal Voicings arising from the pentatonic scales extracted from
the "C" Natural Major Scale. But in order to not get confused by too many chords on the
guitar fretboard, let's use the guide chords from the "5" Vertical Fretboard Zones to help us
(C6 & Am7). We can relate each quartal chord belonging from the pentatonic scale with one
of the guide chords, remembering that we can visualize them from the top note voice or
from the root note ( the intervals are marked with an arrow below and above the chords).

When we are comping with the guitar, we most often use the chords starting from the 3rd,
4th and 5th strings, because the chords rooted from the 6th string might not work.
Sometimes, even the chords starting from the 5th string might not work if used in low areas
of the instrument. Also, sometimes the 4 note quartal chords must be replaced by the 3
note quartal chords.
However, it is always good to know all of them starting from all the strings, because they
can help us to better visualize the guitar fretboard. So in order to better guide us, we will
use again the 5 Fretboard Zones we have learned previously. All the intervals of each zone
are related with a determined chord. In other words, part of them we visualize using C6 and the
other ones using Am.

Attention:

Many quartal tetrad chords presented above might not work well, not only because they are
voiced too low, but also because they contain to many notes, and for this type of chord
structure (quartal voicings) it is not the best voicing choice.


Knowing all the possibilities of quartal tetrads starting from each string is part of the
fretboard visualization process that we must improve on everyday if we want to improvise
and harmonize better.

215                                            2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
Modal Quartal Chord Voicings                                                                                          4668




Below we have some quartal block chord ideas built from the “C” major scale. Depending
on the bass note used over them, we can have a chord sequence that represents a
determined scale mode.We will call this: “Modal Quartal Chord Voicings”.

So let’s get a sequence of chords in the key of “C” major for example:


                                                                              7
      Dmi 74          Emi 74                  Fmaj7(#4)                 G4                    Fmaj7(#4)
        œ
         j              œ                          œœ                     œœ 3                œœ         œœ
 & 44 œœœ ‰         ‰ œœœ           Ó               œœ       ‰      ‰      œœ         ‰        œœ         œœ
                        J                            J                      J                 J
               5fr.               7fr.         1             8fr.                     10fr.   1                8fr.
           2                 2                     23                                               23
                                                         4                        4                      4




Now let’s consider the idea of having any note belonging to the “C” major scale as a bass
note possibility. For example, if we play the bass note “E” continuously over the sequence of
chords above, we would have a “E" Phrygian chord sequence. If we play the bass note “D”
continuously, we would have a “D" Dorian chord sequence, and so on. In other words, now
                                 68


we have not only a chord representing a mode from the major scale, but a chord sequence
representing it.
                      46




This concept is very useful when we play single chord songs such as “Impressions”, the Jirst
part of "Take Five", “So what” and “A Love Supreme” just to give you some examples.
However, we can also use these modal block chords over some chord porgressions, giving
each chord a separated modal treatment. Of course the quartal chords built from a major
scale cannot cover all the chord possibilities we need, but most part of them.
For example at the end of this chapter we will learn how to use quartal chords over altered
chords. It is important to understand that it is best to mix quartal chord voicings with other
chord structures. But for now let's concentrate on learning all we can about the quartal
voicing world.
The examples on the next page are also built from the “C” major scale. Memorize and play
them everytime using a different bass note. By doing this we can have an Ionian, Dorian,
Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian or Locrian chord sequences.

Attention:
To improvise over Polymodal Quartal Chord voicings we can use the minor pentatonic or
the minor blues scale (in the cases above we use "D" Minor Pentatonic or "D" Minor Blues
scale). However, we must be careful when using the pentatonic scale over Locrian chord
voicings, because the perfect 5th of the scale does not belong to this mode. So, in order to
solve this problem, we can play the Minor Blues scale over Locrian chord voicings
emphasizing the #4.

Although we can visualize the intervals of each chord through the top voice or through its
lower note, we will always give preference to the visualization using the lower notes to
guide us. Never lose sight of the guide chords, because in the exercises on the following
pages, we will combine the guide chords with several different modes.

Attention:
1) Never lose the guide chords from your view, and visualize each chord by its root note
2) Lower voiced chords might not work as comping chords
3) The chord symbols for inverted quartal chords will be simple letters

        Harmonizing the
       Minor Blues Scale
      using Quartal Chords
               68
          46




243        2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
As we know, the pentatonic and the blues scales have a deep connection with quartal                      4668




harmony because they form quartal chords. Although they are very similar scales, the
minor blues scale has one additional note (the “blue note”= #4) and for that reason we
have to change the way we harmonize it using quartal voicings.

Minor Pentatonic Scale Quartal Voicings
Notice that when we harmonize the Minor Pentatonic scale using quartal chord voicings,
we are required to use the diminished 4th (major 3rd) in some chords, because we cannot
use notes not belonging to the scale. (they are marked with an arrow).

                          ⇓                                                         ⇓
                                                               ww                   w        b b7ww
                           ww                 b b www                          b b ww          w
                                                                                    5

        b ww
          b7                                     b3             4

&                                                               w
                           1


           w              bw

Minor Blues Scale Quartal Voicings
To harmonize the minor blues scale, we use the same quartal chord shape (1, 4, b7), where
the scale notes will always be on the top voice of each chord. By doing this, we give
strength to the chord melody, since they sound like "power chords" as they contain
intervals of a 5th and 4th between each note.

But using the same chord shape we are required to use some notes not belonging to the
scale, but they do not cause any harmonic problem because they are just part of the chord
shapes that we are using to harmonize them with.
                                 68


The idea to use the same chord shape harmonizing all the scale notes can be explained by
the 3 chromatic notes contained within the minor blues scale (4,#4, 5), because in this case
                    46




a chromatic sequence of notes require us to use the same quartal chord voicing for both. By
doing this we will let only the 2nd chord from the sequence use different interval structure
(Eb, G, C = 1, b4, 6).

Therefore, in order to make the whole sequence of blues scale chord voicings sound better,
we use the same quartal chord shape (1, 4, b7) to harmonize all the notes from the minor
blues scale, even using notes not belonging to it. See the example on the next page:
                   replaced                                chromatic chord sequence
                 chord voicing                          -------------------------------

Minor Blues Scale Quartal Voicings                                                                                     4668




(Extended Visualization)
The exercise below is in the key of C minor on purpose, because the order of the 5 fretboard
zones will change places if compared with the ones we have been using to visualize the
guitar fretboard until now (Cmaj7 & Am7). Notice that the ?irst Cm chord that appears is on
the 3rd fret, which in C major we call the 1st zone. However, the Cm on the 3rd fret has the
same chord shape as Am on the 12th fret, which can cause some confusion. It is important
to understand that the zones themselves never change, but their number will change from
key to key, depending on the ?irst chord we have on the fretboard. In the case of Cm key, the
?irst zone will be related with a minor chord and not with a major chord as in the key of C
major. It is very important to remember that in the case of the minor blues scale, we only
visualize chords from the top voice.

Note: The lower notes might sound not good.

all the notes belonging to a G altered chord. It is important to understand that if we can
apply a determined scale over a determined chord, it means that we can apply all the

Dorian Pentatonic Scale vs Altered                                                                                                          4668




The Dorian Pentatonic Scale contains two different chord shapes, since we use a mix of
quartal chords belonging from two different scales: "Bb" minor blues scale and the altered
scale, forming what we call “Dorian pentatonic scale" (this is just a name, do not worry
about this). Notice that we are using a chromatic chord that works as a kind of “blue note”
for the sequence (marked with an arrow), and also that we have two inverted major chords
(marked with an arrow), that in theory does not belong to the quartal chord harmony.
However, let’s remember that the quartal harmony allows the diminished 4th sometimes
because of the type of scale used. Therefore, we can consider these two inverted major
triad chords as being part of the quartal harmony.

Note: the 2nd chord voicing of each exercise below can only be used as a passing chord
over G7alt. We have chosen 2 different options on the fretboard. See below:

  Study Advice:
  Every Quartal Chord Voicing possibility we have learned until now, must be studied
  separately in order to be incorporated into our playing. We strongly recommend to study
  in one key for sometime, then after visualizing the possibilities in the key you have chosen,
  go ahead with other keys. Remember that we do not have to memorize all the possibilities
  presented in this book. Memorize the ones you like, take your time and enjoy each new
  “color possibility”.


259                                           2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
Harmonic Minor Quartal Chord Voicings                                                                                                                          4668




As we know, the Harmonic Minor scale creates its own dominant chord because of the
major 7th contained within it. Therefore, it means that if we use the "C" harmonic minor
scale quartal chords, we can have a G7 (b9, b13) chord, which can be a perfect dominant
that leads to a major or minor chords.

However, some chord voicings must be used carefully because they contain avoid notes or
just don't sound good. Remember that not everything that is possible is the best choice. So
see the new chord voicing possibilities below:

  The Power of the Dorian Quartal Voicings                                                                                                                            4668




  Usually the dorian chords are only related with minor chords. However, it can be used in a
  way much more sophisticated if we apply some "harmonic tricks". First of all let's
  understand the connection between dorian and dominant 7th chords leading to major or
  minor key. So let's use a G7 chord as an example. Follow these steps:
  1) G7 = Db7 (tritone substitution)
  2) If considered as a mixolydian chord, the Db7 can be related to Abm7, which will give us
    a dorian sequence.
  3) Now we have three chords that can replace each other but not being exactly the same:
    G7 = Db7 = Abm7
  4) As soon as we have a dorian sequence ( Abm7 & Db7), there will be a momentary key
    that can give us its major scale quartal chords. In the case here, we have Gb major
    quartal chord family used over G7.

  interchange concept to make it a lydian chord for a moment. It gives a very tasty ;lavor to

  Minor II/V7/I Quartal Block Chords Possibilities:                                                                                                           4668




  • Dø
  We can use 3 different quartal chord families over a"D" half diminished chord. Two of them
  are derived from two different major scales: “Eb” major and “Db” major, and the last one is
  derived from a melodic minor scale: F melodic minor.
  Dø locrian vs D7(#9)
  The “Eb” major quartal chord family brings the locrian sound to Dø. However the "Db"
  major quartal family is quite "tricky" because we transformed the Dø into D7(#9) chord,
  giving it a blues vibe. Then using the tritone substitution for D7(#9), we can Aind Ab7(13),
  that we can consider mixolydian. Therefore, having this mixolydian chord, we can Aind the
  "Db" major scale quartal chord voicings. See the two possibilities of quartal chord voicings
  over Dø below.

  Note: Be careful of the lower notes. They can make the chord sound undesirable.

  Eb major scale quartal chord family: 4th String Chords

  G7 leading to Cm:
  On the Vth degree of a minor cadence, we can use all the possibilities we have learned for
  dominant 7th chords, except with the mixolydian chord voicings, which can only be used
  when they are leading to major chords.
  A dominant chord that is used incorrectly most of the time is the lydian dominant (also
  called mixolydian #4). It can only be used over dominant 7th chords that are not leading to
  any other chord. The only exception is when we have a sequence of many dominant 7th
  chords one after another just like the example below:

      • ⎟⎟           C7   ⎟                 F7          ⎟             B b7          ⎟            E b7 ⎟                    A b7           ⎟        D b7 ⎟⎟

Extended Major & Minor II/V/I Block Chord Ideas
Now that we have learned many types of quartal chord voicings for each chord from the
major and minor II/V7/I progressions, it is time to add "new colors" to our block chord
ideas by mixing quartal chords with non quartal chord voicings. So make sure you know
all the subjects before you start.


The following exercises on the next page contain:

1) Triads
2) Tetrads
3) Quartal Chords
4) Chord Inversions
5) Tritone Substitutions


The following block chord ideas are great examples of giving us a better idea of how to
                            68


build our own ideas, using the concepts we have been learning up until now. But
remember they should be memorized and not just analyzed in order to become natural
and easy to play.
                    46




It is important to understand that we will be learning two different things at the same
time: chord ideas and rhythmic ideas which we will call "groove ideas". Therefore we can
use block chords applying another groove (rhythm) or use one of the groove ideas
extracted from one of the examples but apply different chords.



How to Improve your Rhytmic Ideas:

The best thing we can do is to listen to "Big Bands" as often as possible, because the
"grooves" are very clear and easy to understand. However, in order to make them become
part of us, we should memorize the songs we like, always singing with the recordings.
